intro.why: Most failed ML projects solved the wrong problem or optimised the wrong number. Requirements engineering links what the business wants to what the model predicts and how success will be measured, before any data is collected.
prereq: Classification metrics (precision, recall) at a basic level

sections.title: When to use machine learning
sections.plain: Use ML for problems that are intrinsically hard, big, or keep changing.
sections.body:
Case (after Hulten)Why rules failExample
Intrinsically hard problemsAmbiguity, sarcasm, context and cultural nuance make fixed rules impossible; grammar rules and dictionaries fail on real-world variabilityUnderstanding human language
Big problemsRule-based systems become unmanageable; ML learns and adapts rules from data and scalesRecommending songs to millions of users from tens of millions of tracks
Time-changing problemsPatterns evolve; a rule like "flag transactions above ₹50,000 at night" goes stale and adversaries adaptFraud detection

The big-data deluge (enormous volumes of posts, searches, messages, transactions and sensor readings produced every minute) is what makes learning from data possible, and also what makes hand-written rules impractical at scale. Conversely, when a problem is precisely specified and stable (tax calculation, validation rules), ordinary code is cheaper, clearer and easier to test.

sections.title: Requirements engineering for probabilistic systems
sections.plain: Translate high-level goals into measurable, data-aware and model-aware specifications.
sections.body:
Traditional systemsML systems
Deterministic: same input → same outputProbabilistic: output depends on data and learned patterns

Requirements must therefore cover:

  • Data quality and availability: what data exists, how good it is, who labels it.
  • Model behaviour under uncertainty: acceptable error rates, what happens on mistakes, confidence handling.
  • Continuous learning and updates: how often to retrain, how to detect drift.
Definition. Requirements engineering in ML systems is about translating high-level goals into measurable, data-aware and model-aware specifications.

sections.title: Goals at four levels
sections.plain: Organisation, product, user and model goals must align, and sometimes conflict.
sections.body:
A goal is a desired outcome of the overall system, aligned across model, system, user and organisational levels and ideally measurable. Model accuracy alone is insufficient: a chatbot's goal is not only "answer questions" but also generate leads, reduce cost and improve user experience.

Goal typeFocusAnswersTypical objectivesMeasured byE-commerce example
OrganisationalBusiness outcomesWhy are we building this?Revenue, profit, market shareKPIs: revenue growth, retention, churnIncrease overall sales revenue by 20%
ProductProduct behaviour and valueWhat should the product achieve?Help users solve problems quicklyTask success rate, feature usageRecommend relevant products
UserNeeds and satisfactionWhat do users want to accomplish?Accurate answers, easy task completionSatisfaction, completion rateFind desired products quickly and easily
ModelML performanceHow well does the model predict?Classify correctly, detect fraud accuratelyAccuracy, precision, recall, F1High click-through rate

Relationships. Goals are hierarchical: model and user goals serve product goals, which serve organisational goals. They can support each other (accuracy improves user experience) or conflict (accuracy vs latency, cost vs quality), so requirements need explicit trade-offs and priorities.

sections.title: From goals to decisions, questions and predictions
sections.plain: Goal ← supported by decisions ← informed by questions ← answered by predictions.
sections.body:
Starting from the goals of an organisation and its people:

  1. Explore the decisions people routinely make to further those goals.
  2. Ask which decisions could be supported by predictions.
  3. Ask which predictions can be produced with machine learning.

Goal ← supports ← Decision ← informs ← Question ← answers ← ML predictions

This chain was formalised in the conceptual modelling notation GR4ML.

sections.title: GR4ML business view (why)
sections.plain: Who needs ML and why: actors, strategic goals, indicators, decisions, questions, insights.
sections.body:
Why GR4ML. Organisations struggle to apply ML effectively; there is a gap between business needs and ML solutions; projects span requirements, data, algorithms and deployment; a structured approach is needed. GR4ML (from the University of Toronto) is a conceptual modelling framework supporting elicitation, design and development of ML solutions. Its core idea: ML is not just algorithms; business, analytics and data must be aligned, and GR4ML connects the three through three views: Business (why), Analytics design (what) and Data preparation (how).

Business view aims: elicit and clarify ML requirements in business context; support analysis such as prioritisation; align business and analytics strategies.

ElementMeaning
ActorStakeholder or user who drives decisions and needs insights
Strategic goalHigh-level business objective
IndicatorMetric evaluating whether a strategic goal is achieved
Decision goalA decision needed to fulfil a strategic goal
Question goalA question that must be answered to support a decision
InsightData-driven answer or finding that addresses a question

Relationships: a strategic goal can be decomposed (AND/OR) into 0..* decision goals; indicators evaluate goals; actors desire goals; insights answer question goals; influences (+/−) link elements.

Credit-risk example. Actor case workers desire the strategic goal process applications, evaluated by the indicator average resolution time. It is AND-decomposed into the decision goal decision on credit application, which needs the question goal what will be the credit risk of the current application?, answered by the insight credit-risk predictive model: type predictive model; input applicant profile; output credit risk (High/Low); usage per instance; update frequency monthly (retrained every month on newer data); learning period the last 48 months of data.

sections.title: GR4ML analytics design view (what)
sections.plain: What analytics is needed: goals, candidate algorithms, softgoals and their trade-offs.
sections.body:
Defines the type of analytics (descriptive, diagnostic, predictive, prescriptive), selects algorithms and techniques, and records trade-offs. Aims: explore alternative approaches; design ML experiments and identify trade-offs; support algorithm selection and monitor performance over time.

ElementMeaning
Analytics goalThe analytical objective (what insight must be generated)
Description / prediction / prescription goalUnderstand patterns / forecast unknown outcomes / recommend optimal actions
AlgorithmA computational method that performs an analytics goal
SoftgoalQuality attribute (e.g. accuracy, interpretability) influencing algorithm choice
Influence+ or − effect of an algorithm on a softgoal

Credit-risk example. Analytics goal classification of applicant profile, evaluated by indicators accuracy and precision. Candidate algorithms: support vector machine, Naive Bayes, decision trees. Softgoals: robustness, interpretability of the model, tolerance to missing values. Typical influences: decision trees help interpretability (+) and cope with missing values; SVMs tend to hurt interpretability (−) but help robustness. The view does not hide the conflict: it documents it so the choice is deliberate (a regulator requiring explanations would favour the tree).

sections.title: GR4ML data preparation view (how) and all three together
sections.plain: How data is prepared: entities, preparation tasks, operators and data flows.
sections.body:
Defines data sources and features, transformations and cleaning, tables and attributes. Aims: support sharing and reuse of prepared data assets; raise data awareness among analytics users; give data engineers a reference for preparation activities.

ElementMeaning
EntityA data object or table used as input/output
Data preparation taskAn operation turning raw data into usable form
OperatorMethod/function executing a preparation step
Data cleaningRemoves noise, missing values and inconsistencies
Data reductionReduces size or dimensionality while keeping information
Algorithm (in this view)Technique within preprocessing (normalisation, encoding)
MechanismUnderlying implementation of a data operation

Credit-risk example. Entity applicant profile {applicant ID (key), age, checking-account balance, savings-account balance, employment status, number of existing credits, credit risk (label)} flows through normalisation → join → filter (SELECT applicant_id, age, … WHERE country = 'CA').

Putting it together: the prepared data (data view) feeds the algorithms (analytics view), whose output is the insight that answers the question behind the decision that serves the strategic goal (business view). Code example ex1 encodes the business view as objects and shows the indicator turning from red (3.1 days) to green (1.36 days) if 60% of decisions are automated (an illustrative assumption).

sections.title: Measures, and accuracy vs precision of measurement
sections.plain: A good measure relates to a goal, is objective and is practical; it must be accurate and precise.
sections.body:
A measure (often called a metric) is a method or standard format for measuring something, such as a classifier's false-positive rate or lines of code written per week. A good measure directly relates to a goal, is quantifiable and objective, and is practical to collect. Example: goal "improve chatbot usefulness" → task success rate, user satisfaction score, conversation completion rate.

PropertyQuestionExample
Accuracy of a measurementHow closely do measured values, on average, represent the real value? (correctness)Does our satisfaction score reflect users' actual satisfaction?
Precision of a measurementHow reliably does the process give the same result, right or wrong? (consistency)Repeatedly asking users gives varying scores

The classic target picture has four cases: accurate and precise (tight cluster on the bullseye), precise but inaccurate (tight cluster off-centre: systematic bias), accurate but imprecise (scattered around the centre), and neither. Code example ex2: a leading survey question with 400 respondents is very precise (spread 0.03 between repeated surveys) but biased by +1.2; a neutral question with 8 respondents is unbiased but imprecise (spread 0.68); a neutral question with 400 respondents is both. (The −0.06 offset in the last case comes from clipping scores to the 0–10 scale.)

Do not confuse these with precision as a classification metric (TP/(TP+FP)); here the words describe the quality of a measurement process.

sections.title: Further insights and misconceptions
sections.body:
• "The requirement is 95% accuracy." Without the data, slices, error costs and baseline, that number is meaningless; accuracy can also be misleading on imbalanced data.
  • "Model goals are the goals." CTR can rise while satisfaction and revenue fall (e.g. clickbait recommendations).
  • "GR4ML is just documentation." Its value is forcing the team to connect each prediction to a decision someone actually makes.
  • "Use ML whenever data exists." Stable, precise rules are better as code.

code.explain: Models the credit-risk business view (strategic goal, indicator, decision, question, insight) as objects, prints the goal tree with indicator status, and recomputes the indicator for an illustrative automation scenario.
mistakes: Indicators without targets (no way to say green or red).
Insights with no owner or update frequency.
code.notes: Real teams keep such models in requirement documents or tools; the value is traceability from model to goal.

code.title: Accuracy vs precision of a survey measure
code.explain: Repeats three survey designs 200 times and separates bias (accuracy) from spread between repeats (precision).
mistakes: Confusing measurement precision with the classification metric precision.
Increasing sample size to fix bias (it only fixes imprecision).
code.notes: Pilot your measures before using them as success criteria.
code.code:
# Accuracy vs precision of a measurement: a satisfaction survey measured repeatedly
import numpy as np
rng = np.random.default_rng(1)
true_satisfaction = 7.0           # what we want to measure (0-10)
designs = {
    "leading question, big sample": dict(bias=+1.2, noise=0.6, n=400),
    "neutral question, tiny sample": dict(bias=0.0, noise=2.0, n=8),
    "neutral question, big sample": dict(bias=0.0, noise=2.0, n=400),
}
print(f"{'survey design':32s} mean_of_runs  bias   spread_between_runs")
for name, d in designs.items():
    runs = [np.clip(true_satisfaction + d['bias'] + d['noise'] * rng.normal(size=d['n']), 0, 10).mean() for _ in range(200)]
    runs = np.array(runs)
    print(f"{name:32s} {runs.mean():12.2f}  {runs.mean() - true_satisfaction:+.2f}  {runs.std():.3f}")
